extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy, rhetoric, and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Bacon's criteria for intellectual virtues and defects (wit, judgement, prudence, madness, knowledge types, power, honour) as laid out in an early-modern philosophical essay. Useful for evaluating modes of thought, discourse quality, and social worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Vertue Defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Vertue generally ... is somewhat that is valued for eminence; and consisteth in comparison. And by Vertues INTELLECTUALL, are always understood such abilityes of the mind, as men praise, value, and desire should be in themselves; and go commonly under the name of a Good Witte.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtues are comparative and socially valued qualities. Intellectual virtues are those mental abilities praised and desired by people; the term 'wit' can refer to a general good mind or to a particular ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Wit
rubrics_metrics.description: This NATURALL WITTE ... consisteth principally in two things; Celerity Of Imagining (that is, swift succession of one thought to another;) and Steddy Direction to some approved end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural wit arises from use and experience without formal method or instruction. Evaluation should consider both speed of imagination and steadiness of direction toward an end; lack of either yields defects like dulness or errant digressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dulnesse (slow imagination)
rubrics_metrics.description: A slow Imagination, maketh that Defect, or fault of the mind, which is commonly called DULNESSE, Stupidity, and sometimes by other names that signifie slownesse of motion, or difficulty to be moved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow associative speed is identified as a cognitive defect; it reduces inventive or responsive capacity. Distinguish dulness (slowness) from other faults rooted in passion or education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Wit / Good Fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Those that observe their similitudes, in case they be such as are but rarely observed by others, are sayd to have a Good Wit; by which, in this occasion, is meant a Good Fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good fancy is valued for finding rare or apt similitudes and producing apt metaphors and novel adornments of style. However, fancy without direction can become digressive or manic; it must be tied to purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: They that observe their differences, and dissimilitudes ... are said to have a Good Judgement: and particularly in matter of conversation and businesse ... this Vertue is called DISCRETION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good judgement emphasizes distinguishing and discerning differences, especially regarding times, places, and persons. It is central to method, truth, and choice (e.g., in history or counsel) and can stand alone as a virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Discretion of times, places, and persons, necessary to a good Fancy, ... this Vertue is called DISCRETION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretion governs appropriateness of speech and conduct in public or solemn contexts. Without discretion, even brilliant fancy is judged as folly. Examples: certain metaphors or playful wordplay acceptable in familiar company are inappropriate in sermons or before dignified persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: When the thoughts of a man, that has a designe in hand, running over a multitude of things, observes how they conduce to that designe; ... This wit of his is called PRUDENCE; and dependeth on much Experience, and Memory of the like things, and their consequences heretofore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudence is practical judgement about means to an end, grounded in experience and memory. It varies less across people of equal age because experience quantities are similar; it applies to governing families, states, or other particular businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft (crooked wisdom)
rubrics_metrics.description: To Prudence, if you adde the use of unjust, or dishonest means ... you have that Crooked Wisdome, which is called CRAFT; which is a signe of Pusillanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft is prudence tainted by unjust means prompted by fear or want. It is morally defective (short-sighted shifting, versutia) despite being effective. Use of dishonesty or usury-like maneuvers indicates craft rather than true virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired Wit (Reason & Science)
rubrics_metrics.description: As for Acquired Wit, (I mean acquired by method and instruction,) there is none but Reason; which is grounded on the right use of Speech; and produceth the Sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquired wit refers to reasoned, methodical knowledge and science, obtained by instruction and method. Evaluate by clarity of argument and demonstrative consequences rather than speed or fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions as Causes of Difference of Wits
rubrics_metrics.description: The causes of this difference of Witts, are in the Passions: ... The Passions that most of all cause the differences of Wit, are principally, the more or lesse Desire of Power, of Riches, of Knowledge, and of Honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different dominant passions direct the imagination and judgement, producing differing styles of wit. Assessments of intellectual character should account for motivational drivers — primarily desire of power and its derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giddinesse and Madnesse (passion-based defects)
rubrics_metrics.description: To have weak Passions, is Dulnesse; and to have Passions indifferently for every thing, GIDDINESSE, and Distraction; and to have stronger, and more vehement Passions for any thing, than is ordinarily seen in others, is that which men call MADNESSE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifies cognitive defects along a spectrum: dulness (weak passions), giddiness (indifference), and madness (excessive passions). Use this to diagnose whether cognitive anomalies stem from paucity, diffusion, or excess of desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rage (madness from pride, jealousy, revenge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride, subjecteth a man to Anger, the excesse whereof, is the Madnesse called RAGE, and FURY. ... excessive desire of Revenge, when it becomes habituall, hurteth the organs, and becomes Rage: That excessive love, with jealousie, becomes also Rage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rage is madness manifesting as excessive anger arising from pride, jealousy, revenge, or over-attachment to one's opinion. It may become habitual and physiologically damaging; evident in both individuals and mobs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melancholy (dejection-based madness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dejection, subjects a man to causelesse fears; which is a Madnesse commonly called MELANCHOLY, apparent also in divers manners; as in haunting of solitudes, and graves; in superstitious behaviour; and in fearing some one, some another particular thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melancholy is characterized by dejection leading to baseless fears, solitude-seeking, superstition, and other odd behaviours. Assess behavioural markers (haunting graves, superstitions) to identify this form of madness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madness as over-appearing Passion / 'Private Spirit'
rubrics_metrics.description: This opinion of Inspiration, called commonly, Private Spirit, begins very often, from some lucky finding of an Errour generally held by others; ... they presently admire themselves; as being in the speciall grace of God Almighty, who hath revealed the same to them supernaturally, by his Spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon treats claims of private divine inspiration or possession as a kind of madness stemming from inflated self-admiration after finding an error. Distinguish genuine insight from delusional attribution to spirits; social/mass manifestations (prophets, daemoniacks) amplify effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Speech / Absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: That abuse of words ... is, when men speak such words, as put together, have in them no signification at all; but are fallen upon by some, through misunderstanding of the words they have received, and repeat by rote; by others, from intention to deceive by obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies unintelligible scholastic or obscure language as a fault (absurdity). Examples include convoluted scholastic sentences and metaphysical jargon (e.g., abstruse discussions of Transubstantiation) that produce speech with 'no signification at all.' This is counted among kinds of madness or folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of Fact vs Knowledge of Consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: There are of KNOWLEDGE two kinds; whereof one is Knowledge Of Fact: the other Knowledge Of The Consequence Of One Affirmation To Another. The former is ... Sense and Memory, and is Absolute Knowledge ... The later is called Science; and is Conditionall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish testimonial/empirical knowledge (sense & memory, required of witnesses) from demonstrative/scientific knowledge (reasoning about consequences, required of philosophers). Use appropriate epistemic standard depending on the role: witness vs philosopher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registers: History vs Science
rubrics_metrics.description: The Register of Knowledge Of Fact is called History. ... The other, is Civill History; which is the History of the Voluntary Actions of men in Common-wealths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifies historical register: Natural history (facts of nature) vs Civil history (voluntary human actions). Treat history as the archive of facts distinct from books of demonstrative science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of the Sciences (classification of Philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science, that is, Knowledge of Consequences; which is called also PHILOSOPHY ... A. Consequences from Accidents of Bodies Naturall (NATURALL PHILOSOPHY) ... Mathematiques (GEOMETRY, ARITHMETIQUE) ... ASTRONOMY, GEOGRAPHY ... ENGINEERS, ARCHITECTURE, NAVIGATION ... PHYSIQUES ... ETHIQUES ... POETRY ... RHETORIQUE ... LOGIQUE
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a hierarchical map of sciences: first philosophy (knowledge of consequences) divided into natural philosophy (quantity, motion, qualities), mathematica, cosmography, mechanics, meteorology, optics, music, ethics, rhetoric, logic, etc. Use this taxonomy to situate a discipline by its subject-matter (quantity, motion, qualities, political bodies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power (definition and types)
rubrics_metrics.description: The POWER of a Man ... is his present means, to obtain some future apparent Good. And is either Originall, or Instrumentall. Naturall Power, is the eminence of the Faculties of Body, or Mind ... Instrumentall are those Powers ... acquired by these, or by fortune, are means and Instruments to acquire more: as Riches, Reputation, Friends, and the Secret working of God, which men call Good Luck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate power as present capacity to secure future goods. Distinguish natural (personal faculties: strength, prudence, eloquence) from instrumental powers (riches, reputation, friends). Recognize compounded power (union of many) as greatest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worth (value of a man)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Value, or WORTH of a man, is as of all other things, his Price; that is to say, so much as would be given for the use of his Power: and therefore is not absolute; but a thing dependant on the need and judgement of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worth is relational and context-dependent (e.g., a military commander more valuable in wartime). Assessment of worth should consider the buyer's needs and judgments rather than the subject's self-rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity (public worth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The publique worth of a man, which is the Value set on him by the Common-wealth, is that which men commonly call DIGNITY. And this Value of him by the Common-wealth, is understood, by offices of Command, Judicature, publike Employment; or by Names and Titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dignity is the community's formal valuation via offices, titles, and employment. It is socially conferred and can vary by polity; use institutional markers (office, title) as signals of public worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to Honour and Dishonour (manifestations of value)
rubrics_metrics.description: To pray to another, for ayde of any kind, is to HONOUR ... To obey, is to Honour ... To give great gifts to a man, is to Honour him ... To neglect, is to Dishonour. ... To praise, magnifie, or call happy, is to Honour; To revile, mock, or pitty, is to Dishonour. ... To believe, to trust, to rely on another, is to Honour him; signe of opinion of his vertue and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a detailed list of actions that constitute honouring (prayer for aid, obedience, gifts, deference, praise, trust, employment, imitation, etc.) and dishonouring (neglect, refusal, revilement, imitation of enemies). Use these behavioural markers to judge social valuation and status.
